04 · Read & review

The transcript

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

The first material Fiona Bell could describe from the folder marked “Payment exceptions — 2011” was not a scandalous ledger but an administrative glossary. Emma felt a flicker of disappointment before recognising its value. A category could not be interpreted fairly until she understood the institution's rules for assigning it.

The introductory sheet listed several circumstances in which an expected payment might be classified as an exception: incomplete supporting evidence, changes in travel arrangements and transfers returned by a bank. None of those descriptions implied misconduct. Equally, their routine appearance in a manual could not establish that every subsequent case had been handled properly.

Fiona had no verified case count and had not reconciled the relevant entries with remittance or banking records. She cautioned that an exception might be resolved through a later transaction, but that this had not been confirmed for any particular student.

Sarah suggested they might finally have evidence of unpaid grants. Emma rejected the inference. What they had was evidence that the trust anticipated circumstances in which an authorised payment might not proceed normally. The real questions were frequency, cause and eventual outcome.

She revisited Helen Ward's redacted copy of the selection notice. It supplied a limited account of one successful decision, subject to further documentation. Helen had now asked her cousin about historical banking records. None had been located, and the cousin's recollection of any payment was uncertain. Crucially, the absence of an old statement did not establish that the account had never been credited. Emma accepted the family's reluctance to undertake a broader search.

One feature of the exception guidance offered a method. Administrators were instructed to enter a follow-up reference when a problem was resolved. If the surviving records permitted the initial and subsequent entries to be matched, Emma might be able to distinguish a temporarily interrupted transfer from a permanently outstanding one. Yet the failure to locate such a link in an incomplete archive would not itself prove that a payment remained unsettled.

Sarah proposed requesting aggregate figures for unresolved exceptions. Emma refined the proposal. They needed totals defined by the scheme's own categories and dates, alongside an explanation of missing or damaged records. Otherwise an apparent discrepancy might result from surviving paperwork rather than from anything that happened to students.

Late in the afternoon Fiona reported an additional notation in the preliminary register: “manual approval”. Neither the reasons for the notation nor the authorised signatories had been checked. Emma recognised the phrase as a possible route back to the anonymous caller's insistence that she examine payment approvals, not merely meeting minutes. But the caller's knowledge and intentions remained unverified. Two suggestive details did not automatically corroborate one another.

Emma placed three questions beside the notation: What circumstances required manual approval? Who had authority to provide it? Was the subsequent transfer completed?

A form could establish a procedure; a signed authorisation, if genuine, could establish a decision; a bank record might establish a transaction. Those were different kinds of proof. For the first time, though, she could see how all three might be brought together without exposing a former student's identity.

She closed the file on the phrase “manual approval”, treating it not as an accusation but as the next testable question.
